cards.title: The Identity Anchor Effect
cards.insight: People sustain behavior change more effectively when they reframe desired actions as core to their identity rather than external obligations. A person who views regular exercise as 'being athletic' rather than 'should exercise' achieves greater consistency because identity-based motivation operates at a deeper psychological level than willpower-dependent rules.
cards.takeaway: Choose one habit you want to build and explicitly adopt the identity label that goes with it (e.g., 'I am someone who reads daily'), then make small decisions that reinforce that identity.

cards.title: Friction Design Shapes Default Behavior
cards.insight: Environmental design—adding friction to unwanted actions and removing it from desired ones—outperforms pure motivation. When bad habits require extra steps (moving snacks to a high shelf, turning off app notifications) and good ones are frictionless (water bottle on desk, workout clothes laid out), behavior naturally shifts without constant mental effort.
cards.takeaway: Audit your physical environment this week and add one friction point to a habit you want to reduce and remove one from a habit you want to increase.

cards.title: The Streak Paradox
cards.insight: Tracking visible progress through streaks creates psychological momentum but can backfire—one missed day triggers all-or-nothing collapse. The paradox resolves by focusing on 'never miss twice' rather than 'never miss once,' which preserves identity and motivation even after inevitable lapses.
cards.takeaway: If you track a habit, adopt the rule that one slip is acceptable but two in a row signals you need to troubleshoot, not that you've failed entirely.

cards.title: Habit Stacking: The Attachment Strategy
cards.insight: Attaching a new behavior to an existing routine (brushing teeth, morning coffee, evening walk) exploits established neural pathways rather than requiring willpower for standalone actions. This 'piggyback' approach dramatically improves adoption because it borrows the automaticity already built into your routine.
cards.takeaway: Identify one existing daily habit and choose one small new behavior to chain directly after it—execute it together for the next two weeks before evaluating.
